Comping rhythm: Strum: sixteenths

For guitar, built up a step at a time

This is a lesson on one comping rhythm the Backing Track band plays: Strum: sixteenths. It is built up from 2 simpler patterns, one step at a time, and every step is played by the band and written out as it plays. How the examples work: press ▶ Play, switch players in and out with the buttons beside it, and read what the band will play on the staff underneath: the whole pass is written out when Play starts, before it sounds. The tempo slider at the bottom of the page slows everything down.

All the accompaniment patterns · Comping rhythms

The pattern

The D, D-U, U-D-U strum at double speed, twice in the bar. For slow and medium tempos.

It belongs in Acoustic strum, Straight-eighth rock and Dance pop. Here it is in the acoustic strum style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

Step 1: Strum: down-up eighths

Start with something simpler. Every eighth note, down on the beat and up off it, leaning on 2 and 4.

This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

Step 2: Strum: D, D-U, U-D-U

The strum most songbooks start with: down on 1, down-up on 2, then up, down-up through 3 and 4 (the hand misses the strings on beat 3).

This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

Step 3: Strum: sixteenths, slowly

Now the pattern itself. Compare it with the step before: press each button while the band plays and watch what changes on the staff.

How to play it. The D, D-U, U-D-U strum twice as fast, twice a bar. The hand now moves down-up in sixteenths. Keep it small and from the wrist; start at half tempo.

Step 4: Up to tempo, with the band

The whole band, at 96 beats a minute. Play along, then switch the band’s chord player off and take the part yourself.

Step 5: Two chords in a bar

Harder: now some bars have two chords, two beats each. The pattern keeps its rhythm and changes chord where the bar does: watch the staff for the hit that lands on beat 3.

In other styles

The same comping rhythm in other styles it fits. The other players change; yours does not. Notice how the same part sounds different in a different band.

Straight-eighth rock

Dance pop

How it relates to the other patterns

  • Builds on: Strum: down-up eighths, Strum: D, D-U, U-D-U.
  • Leads to: Groups: eight 3s then four 2s (sixteenths): the patterns that use this one as a step.
  • The same idea elsewhere in the band: Groups: eight 3s then four 2s (sixteenths) (comping rhythm), Hi-hat: sixteenth notes (drum groove), Hi-hat: sixteenths, two hands (drum groove).
  • Plays with, in acoustic strum: Dotted (1, and of 2, 3) (bass line), Pop backbeat (drum groove).
  • Other comping rhythms in the Folk, rock and pop group: Boom-chick / oom-pah-pah, Waltz in one, Ballad: rocking, Ballad: half-broken, Ballad: syncopated, Quarter-note chords, Triplet chords (12/8), Driving eighths.
